```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Nothing here fits a model: the prior checks run in R, and the calibration
# results are those saved by dev/precompute-calibration.R for
# vignette("calibration").
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
results <- readRDS("calibration-results.rds")
# range of coverage of the occupancy slope over the levels of verification
cov_range <- function(model) {
  v <- as.data.frame(results$verification)
  v <- v[v$parameter == "occ_x" & v$model == model, ]
  cov <- purrr::map_dbl(split(v$covered, v$frac_verified), mean)
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(cov), max(cov))
}
```

Before recording starts, three decisions shape what a false-positive
occupancy analysis can deliver: how many sites and occasions, how much to
check by hand, and what to assume about the classifier. This article walks
through the tools in crywolf that inform those decisions, in the order in
which they are usually needed. None of them needs real data; a pilot, the
literature, or a guess stated openly is enough.

## 1. What the classifier is likely to do

The false-positive rate is identified by the checked data, but the gap
between the true-detection and false-positive intercepts also has a prior
(`vignette("crywolf")`). When a random sample of detections from a pilot or
an earlier study was reviewed, its precision, the share of detections that
were true, says roughly where the gap lies. `fp_gap_prior()` turns the counts
into a prior, given rough values of the detection probability at occupied
sites and of occupancy:

```{r gap-prior}
set.seed(1)
pr <- fp_gap_prior(n_true = 46, n_false = 4, p11 = 0.6, psi = 0.5)
pr
```

The sample must be random among the detections at the threshold you will
use. Detections picked for their high scores overstate the precision and
push the prior towards a classifier that errs less than it does.

## 2. What the priors imply for the planned design

A planned design can be written as a simulation: `simulate_fp()` takes the
number of sites, occasions, and verified sites, and plausible rates. With it,
`fp_prior_predictive()` draws parameter values from the priors and shows the
data they would produce, before anything is fitted.

```{r prior-predictive}
plan <- simulate_fp(nsite = 200, nocc = 10, frac_verified = 0.3, seed = 1)
pp <- fp_prior_predictive(plan$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1,
                          random_recorder = FALSE, priors = pr,
                          ndraws = 200, seed = 1)
pp
```

The columns are the share of sites with at least one automated detection,
the share of automated occasions that are detections, and the share of
verified occasions that are detections. If the plausible values for your
system sit in the tails of these distributions, the priors are at odds with
what you expect, and it is better to find out now.

## 3. Whether the design can answer the question

The core risk is a false-positive rate that tracks the same gradient as
occupancy, which biases the occupancy effects (Provete et al., in
preparation). `fp_verification_curve()` simulates that situation for the
design at hand, fits the candidate models, and scores how often their
intervals contain the true slope. `vignette("calibration")` describes the
output; here we use its saved results to read off two things a plan needs:
the precision to expect and the computing cost.

```{r widths}
v <- as.data.frame(results$verification)
v <- v[v$parameter == "occ_x", ]
width <- stats::aggregate(cbind(width = upper - lower) ~ model + frac_verified, v, mean)
width$width <- round(width$width, 2)
width
```

```{r width-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Mean width of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, in 300 sites with 20 occasions and a false-positive rate that tracks the occupancy gradient (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7)."}
ggplot2::ggplot(width, ggplot2::aes(frac_verified, width, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() + ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Fraction of sites verified", y = "Mean interval width",
                colour = "Model") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

In this design, verifying more sites hardly changes the width of the
interval of the slope, and the calibration results show that it does not
remove the bias of the constant-rate model either. Modelling the rate on the
occupancy covariate gives slightly wider intervals, the price of the extra
parameter, but intervals that cover the true slope far more often
(`r cov_range("fp_on_x")` of the time, against `r cov_range("constant")`
for the constant rate). A plan
that relies on verification alone to deal with a confounded false-positive
rate will not work.

```{r cost}
secs <- stats::median(as.data.frame(results$verification)$seconds)
n_fits <- nrow(unique(as.data.frame(results$verification)[c("cell", "model", "rep")]))
c(fits = n_fits, median_seconds_per_fit = round(secs))
```

Each of these fits used 4 chains of 1000 warm-up and 1000 sampling
iterations, run one after another inside each of 8 parallel workers. A run
of this size therefore costs about `r round(n_fits * secs / 8 / 3600, 1)`
hours of wall time on 8 cores. Two chains per fit halve that, with an
effective sample size that is still ample for scoring intervals (see
`?fp_calibrate`).

## 4. Choices that are cheap to make now

* **Occasions.** Shorter occasions (minutes instead of nights) give more
  data per site but are more likely to come in runs, when a calling animal
  is recorded in consecutive minutes. Plan to record the time of each
  occasion, so that runs can be modelled (`vignette("markov")`).
* **What to measure.** A covariate that might drive false positives, such
  as background noise or another species that the classifier confuses with
  the target, is worth recording even if occupancy does not depend on it.
  It can enter the false-positive formula later (`vignette("fp_variation")`).
* **How to check.** Whole-recording annotation (the multiple-methods design)
  and checking flagged clips (the confirmation design) need different files;
  `vignette("birdnet_workflow")` shows both. Draw the checked recordings or
  clips at random.
* **Recorders.** If several recorders are used, keep track of which one made
  each recording, so that differences among them can be modelled as a
  random effect.

## 5. After the data are in

Once a model is fitted to the real data, `fp_calibrate_fit()` repeats the
check of step 3 with the sites, covariates, and verification that were
actually obtained, and with the effect sizes the fit estimated
(`vignette("calibration")`). It answers the question of step 3 for the
study that was done rather than the one that was planned.

## References

Provete, D. B., et al. (in preparation).
